This study evaluates the impact of varying sensor thicknesses and substrate materials on the monolithic microstrip readout detector, designated CLICTD, which employs a small electrode design. By utilizing the simulation software TCAD, we analyzed how these factors influence the detector's temporal and spatial resolution, as well as its electric field distribution. The results indicate that reducing sensor thickness improves time resolution, whereas the choice of substrate material has a negligible effect on this specific parameter. Conversely, spatial resolution benefits from using GaN as the substrate material, which outperforms the standard SiC alternative.

The Self-Coherent Camera (SCC) technique offers a method to correct for high-altitude turbulence by utilizing an internal guide star and waveguide, thereby eliminating the need for external natural or artificial beacons. This study presents the inaugural field deployment of the SCC, conducted via the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics (EAO) testbed in Santa Cruz, California. During this experiment, the SCC operated in tandem with a 1.5-meter adaptive optics system to deliver high-speed wavefront sensing and correction of atmospheric turbulence. The system successfully achieved a correction rate of 2000 Hz, utilizing a 1000-element deformable mirror to manage turbulence across a 1.2° field of view. The results demonstrate that the SCC can effectively isolate and track turbulence cells within a field of view exceeding the coherence diameter ($D_0$) by a factor of ten, with speckle velocities reaching up to 1000 m/s.

This study introduces a new closed-form solution for a four-factor deterministic-shift augmented Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) model, designed to capture the J-curve of interest rate dynamics. We evaluate our proposed framework against various existing term structure models by comparing zero-coupon bond yields and the corresponding implied volatility surface. Furthermore, we utilize this model to simulate various interest rate derivatives, including zero-coupon bonds, forward rate agreements, swaptions, and par swaps, for the purpose of valuation.

Active neutrino oscillations have been confirmed by numerous experiments, yet the long-standing LSND and MiniBooNE anomalies hint at the possible existence of a neutrino mass eigenstate decaying by eV. The presence of such a sterile neutrino would necessitate a fourth right-handed state, modifying the Standard Model and influencing neutrino oscillation dynamics at the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). Operating at a 1,300 km baseline, DUNE is uniquely positioned to probe sterile neutrains in the sub-eV mass range, a sensitivity that standard short-baseline configurations cannot achieve. This study examines DUNE's potential to detect sterile neutrinos through both short and long baselines, analyzing the implications of existing data from MiniBooNE and proposals for an auxiliary short baseline facility. We demonstrate that incorporating data from 10 GeV and 20 GeV beams at 560 m and 600 m would substantially enhance the experiment's oscillation analysis, while the 1,200 km far detector remains capable of providing distinct, complementary constraints on the oscillation parameters.

Meta-analysis serves as a statistical technique to synthesize available research on a particular topic. In this study, we address the issue of accounting for dependencies among effect sizes stemming from the same trial or from correlated covariates. We introduce a new class of robust, two-stage cluster estimators designed to yield unbiased estimates of between-trial variability. These methods are constructed by aggregating random effects using various clustering strategies and are validated through simulation against existing robust techniques. The proposed approaches are subsequently applied to a practical meta-analysis involving the bivariate comparison of two chemotherapy agents against a control in treating colorectal cancer.

Particle-resolved simulations are increasingly utilized to investigate multiphase flows at a mesoscale where individual particles retain their own mass, radius, and drag coefficients, all of which evolve over time. Conventional simulations typically resolve the drag buildup phase within the particle's wake using a single time-step, resulting in a collision duration that is artificially short relative to physical reality. This study introduces an innovative multi-time-step integration technique designed to accurately model the realistic duration of particle collisions. Validation against analytical solutions for one-dimensional wave equations and a case study of gas-solid fluidization demonstrates the method's effectiveness.

This study examines the origins of particles associated with the Unruh and Hawking effects. It is established that such radiation does not emanate from a black hole's surface or interior; rather, the constituent particles constituting the emitted stream originate from outside the black hole.

This study examines the lateral nuclear momentum imbalance within the color dipole framework, a process central to exploring quantum correlations and serving as a signature for the quark-gluon plasma momentum imbalance. Employing both leading-order and next-to-leading-order calculations, we determine that the calculated momentum imbalance aligns well with recent experimental data.

This paper presents $2$ independent proofs demonstrating that the Diophantine equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ possesses $2$ distinct proofs showing that the only whole number solutions to $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ are $2$ independent proofs

This study examines the behavior of an interface separating two viscous, incompressible fluids characterized by distinct densities and viscosities, where one fluid infiltrates the other across a planar boundary. The system operates under the influence of viscous drag, surface tension, and gravitational forces. Employing a weakly non-linear analysis, the study derives an equation for the evolution of amplitude, which incorporates terms for dispersion, dissipation, and forcing. The resulting model reveals a nonlinear instability that emerges when viscous effects dominate over both gravity and surface tension.

As a nonvolatile memory (NVM) technology, NVM offers the advantage of retaining data without power, yet it is vulnerable to bit flips caused by cosmic rays and alpha particles. These single-event upsets (SEUs) can corrupt data, potentially leading to unreliable outcomes in applications. This paper introduces a novel algorithm for ensuring crash reliability in NVM within high-performance computing (HPC) environments. The approach is transparent to users and application logic, requiring no modifications to existing code. By leveraging the inherent parallelism found in large-scale HPC systems, the algorithm employs multiple write operations to mitigate SEUs, thereby enhancing reliability. Experimental results from the BlueHornet supercomputer demonstrate that the method successfully reduces the probability of unrecoverable SEUs to levels below current application requirements.

This study examines the computational methods used to determine structural metrics within information networks. We categorize these approaches into two main categories: those rooted in graph theory and those based on social algebra. We evaluate the computational complexity of each method and analyze the computational requirements for scaling these algorithms to real-world, large-scale networks. Finally, we provide a review of existing frameworks, discussing their strengths and limitations.

The three-body problem is a prototypical chaotic system that serves as a benchmark for investigating how statistical mechanics applies to physical phenomena. This study examines the statistical distribution of Lyapunov exponents in a three-body gravitational system, contrasting these findings with predictions derived from flux-based statistical theory. The results demonstrate a close alignment between our observations and the flux theory, reinforcing the validity of applying statistical methods to chaotic dynamics.

This study examines the suppression of $\mathrm{J}/\psi$ and $\psi(2\mathrm{S})$ mesons in lead–lead collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 5.02\,\mathrm{TeV}$, utilizing data from the ALICE experiment at the LHC. The analysis covers PbPb events alongside $pp$ references at center-of-mass energies of $7\,\mathrm{TeV}$ and $18\,\mathrm{TeV}$, as well as $p\mathrm{Pb}$ and $\mathrm{ppb}$ at $5\,\mathrm{TeV}$. The nuclear modification factor, $A_d$, is determined for midrapidity ($|y| < 0.9$) across various centrality classes, with cross-checks performed in forward rapidity regions ($2.5 < y < 4$ and $-4 < y < -2.5$). The findings are interpreted using a model that incorporates both initial-state charm quark suppression and final-state quenching of charmonia. The data indicate that the measured $\mathrm{J}/\psi$ suppression in the central $pp$ collisions aligns with expectations from quenching alone, whereas the $\psi(2\mathrm{S})$ suppression exceeds quenching predictions, suggesting a significant contribution from cold nuclear matter effects.

We introduce a category of metric spaces that aligns with the requirements of T. Vallentine's pcpo framework for continuous logic, a system designed to accommodate the compactness of the real numbers. This construction is shown to be compact by a modified application of the classical Tychonoff theorem.

This paper introduces a novel approach to the test suite selection problem within software frameworks. The proposed solution is designed to be lightweight, accelerates build cycles, and is applicable to a broad range of scenarios. The selection algorithm operates by modeling the framework's components as a graph, where nodes represent components and edges signify their dependencies. The method then transforms this graph into a system of linear equations over the Galois Field GF(2), solving which yields a valid component subset for execution. The study also examines parallelizing the test suite selection algorithm, demonstrating that the resulting solution vector remains consistent regardless of parallelization. The paper concludes by outlining the implementation of this strategy within the Apache Commons Math library.

This paper introduces a new methodology for detecting suicidal ideation in text by utilizing deep sequential networks. We assessed the efficacy of this approach using the 2018 International Challenge on Detection and Prevention of Suicide from Social Media data. The results indicate that our method surpasses the challenge's baseline and achieves a significant improvement over the best previously submitted entries from that competition.

The IXPE mission, consisting of the Imaging X-ray Polarimeter, represents the inaugural observatory capable of measuring X-ray polarization across 2–5 keV energies. This capability allows for the assessment of both the degree and orientation of polarization, offering a novel method to investigate the magnetic field structures within astrophysical sources. The instrument recently completed observations of the Crab Nebula, a pulsar wind nebula, and the core-collapse supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A). Cas A, a nearby object (~3.4 kpc) characterized by a complex, multi-phase ejecta and remnant core, is expected to emit significant polarized radiation due to the synchrotron emission from its shock-accelerated electrons. This report details the IXPE measurement of Cas A, which detected a mean polarization fraction of 0.31% with a 90% confidence limit of 0.51%. The observed polarization angle varied between 100° and 200° across the 2–5 keV energy band, a variation consistent with predictions from single-temperature thermal models and multi-temperature synchrotron scenarios. Furthermore, the data indicate a slight decline in polarization fraction with increasing energy, a trend that aligns with predictions from multi-temperature synchrotron models and emission arising from a jet within the Cas A remnant.

Let $A$ be a finite set of positive integers. We say $A$ has the EUS property if all sums $a_1 + \dots + a_k$ with $1 \le a_1 \le \dots \le k \le |A|$ are distinct. We show that if $A$ is a random subset of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ where each element is included independently with probability $p = p(n)$, then $A$ satisfies the EUS property with high probability provided $n \ll p \ll n^{1/3}$. This result also applies to high probability to sets $A$ chosen uniformly at random from all subsets of size $(1-o(1))n p$.

We examine the equation of state (EOS) and the sound speed for cold, dense, and magnetized matter containing baryons and electrons. Our analysis focuses on scenarios involving both quark deconfinement and electron capture, which lead to the presence of strange quarks. We employ the MIT bag model alongside a cold, dense, isospin-symmetric electron gas to construct the EOS, subsequently determining the sound speed by applying the standard thermodynamic formula. Our results indicate that the sound speed rises as density increases, reaching a maximum value of approximately $c_s/c = 1/3$ at low densities before declining at higher densities. We further analyze how the bag constant and the electron mass influence this behavior. Additionally, we determine the maximum mass and radius of strange stars by applying the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equations.

This study examines the effects of parameter shifts on squeezing within the Fock space of the new generalized compass state. We demonstrate that varying these parameters alters the wave function's parity and consequently switches the state's quantum behavior between that of a squeezed coherent state and a squeezed thermal state.

This work investigates the interface structure within multiphase flows by introducing a skeleton-based methodology. The primary objective is to develop an effective interface representation that facilitates the characterization of both interface topology and geometry. The study examines the flow of liquid and gas phases, with interfacial features defined through level set functions. Intuitively, the interface skeleton corresponds to the central line of a tubular interface, where the interface itself forms a tube with uniform thickness. Mathematically, it constitutes the locus of points maintaining a non-zero minimal distance to the interface, effectively representing a refined version of the medial axis. While prior research has largely concentrated on skeletons within static interfaces, this paper addresses the formulation and computation of skeletons for time-evolving interfaces. The proposed methodology is validated through various simulations, including bubble rise dynamics, droplet deformation, and the generation of Kelvin-Helmholtz waves.

This study introduces a novel mechanical model to investigate the spontaneous rolling motion of certain icosahedral viruses, a phenomenon previously identified in experiments but lacking a theoretical explanation. While this movement was initially hypothesized to facilitate the penetration of host cells, our analysis reveals that the motion is fundamentally driven by a gradient in bending stiffness across the capsid, resulting from asymmetric packaging of the viral genome. The proposed model integrates the gradient bending theory for thin shells with the mechanics of self-rolling, effectively accounting for the observed rolling dynamics. The bending stiffness gradient arises because genomic material is not uniformly distributed; instead, it is localized within three dense clusters separated by regions of relative emptiness. This distribution exerts non-uniform deformation on the protein shell, inducing a self-rolling effect analogous to the motion of a three-lobed wheel. The paper outlines the mechanisms behind this bending asymmetry and quantifies the resulting torque driving the movement, demonstrating that the rolling torque scales with viral size and is substantial enough to overcome viscous resistance in a fluid environment. Furthermore, the study examines the role of capsid proteins known as scaffolding proteins, which assist in genome packaging. The presence of these proteins creates localized bending stiffness variations that can either augment or diminish the overall self-rolling torque, depending on their specific positioning. The findings offer a comprehensive theoretical basis for understanding the physical origins of virus rolling and its potential utility in enhancing host cell entry.

We present findings from a study of 10 deformed disk galaxies in the nearby Local Volume, selected for their prominent U-type warps. These systems were originally identified as U-type warps within galaxy groups or clusters by Butcher & Ostriker (1977), a classification that has remained influential for over four decades. Our analysis reveals that these disks exhibit significant vertical deformations, with $|q|$ values ranging from 0.2 to 0.6. We hypothesize that the physical mechanisms driving these deformations are analogous to those producing jellyfish galaxies, a phenomenon also investigated in this work.

This study establishes a Liouville theorem asserting that any non-trivial Ricci diminutor possessing a Liouville Theorem, the paper proves that any compact manifold cannot support a smooth, positive, non-constant harmonic function under these conditions. The authors further derive a corresponding result for harmonic maps from any complete manifold with a Ricci diminutor of constant scalar curvature into a space form. Additionally, a mean curvature Liouville theorem is proved for immersions of such maps into Euclidean space. As a direct application of these findings, the authors demonstrate the rigidity of harmonic maps with scalar curvature remaining constant, specifically showing they must be trivial when the domain is a Euclidean space or sphere.

First-principles calculations reveal that KBi$_2$, RbBi$_2$, and CsBi$_2$—all of which crystallize in the A-type Laves phase with space group $Fm\overline{3}m$—exhibit a soft vibrational mode at the $\Gamma$ point when the Bi atoms vibrate along the local [111] direction. This mode is chiral in nature, corresponding to the rotation of Bi trimers around the cube corners, and lies just below the acoustic branch. Its low frequency indicates strong stability against rotational distortion, suggesting these materials could serve as potential candidates for chiral vibration applications.

We define the Born effective charge $Z^*$ as a metric quantizing the dipole moment change in a metal resulting from the displacement of a single electron. We establish that in a one-dimensional system, the magnitude of this charge is constrained by $|Z^*| \leq v_F/v_s$, where $v_F$ represents the Fermi velocity and $v_s$ the sound velocity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the absolute value $|Z^*|$ directly correlates with the Drude weight, thereby providing a microscopic framework for interpreting the physical significance of this charge.

This study investigates the effects of thermal fluctuations on dissipative fluid turbulence. We demonstrate that the existing theoretical framework for dissipative turbulence, which is applicable to systems like the atmosphere and oceans, can be established by incorporating a temperature-dependent viscosity into the standard shell model. Our results indicate that thermal activity enhances the energy cascade, resulting in elevated dissipation rates. Furthermore, we derive a relationship linking the intensity of thermal disturbance to the mean flow's Reynolds number.

This study introduces a class of insulators exhibiting a magnetoelectric effect that persists even in the absence of an external magnetic field, termed the "geometric magnetoelectric effect." This phenomenon arises from a nonlinear coupling between electric polarization and the magnetization generated by a weak, fluctuating magnetic field, governed by a universal, topological-origin coefficient. We demonstrate that this effect serves as a definitive signature of a novel quantum phase, wherein the magnetization induced by an applied electric field exhibits a half-integer quantized value for the Hall conductivity. This regime, referred to as the half-integer quantum Hall effect, is protected by time-reversal symmetry and can be understood as a gapped variant of the standard quantum Hall effect. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between this emergent magnetization and the Witten effect, suggesting that these systems host fractional magnetic monopoles.

This study introduces a novel mechanism for chaos generation in delay systems, distinguished by its simplicity and the substantial control parameter range it offers. This regime arises from the slow periodic variation of the time lag, resulting in a simplified one-dimensional maximal Lyapunov exponent spectrum. The observed chaotic behavior stems from the interaction between the delay and the system's spectrum, specifically the folding of eigenvalues across the imaginary axis. Notably, the system exhibits "giant" amplification, where minor adjustments to the minimal system parameters trigger drastic shifts in the dispersion ratio. The system's dynamics are analyzed through a delay differential equation featuring linear forcing and a periodically modulated time lag. The resulting state space reveals a coexistence of attractors, including stable periodic orbits and multiple basins of attraction.

The random lambda calculus, a probabilistic extension of the classical lambda calculus, employs fair distribution to split arguments during beta-reduction. Although individual terms within this framework exhibit only a finite number of reductions, they can execute indefinitely. This study introduces global semantics for the random lambda calculus by defining a measure-preserving transformation on the Borel space of infinite reduction sequences for any given lambda term. We demonstrate an equivalence between this approach and an alternative method based on the infinite execution paths of a specific state machine. Furthermore, we establish key properties regarding the convergence of random functions and provide a normal form theory for random lambda terms.

This study introduces Conclusion Robustness, a novel metric for assessing how well a conclusion withstands alterations to its supporting arguments. We demonstrate the applicability of this metric by executing a mining task on sets of engineering design dialogues, where conclusions were derived through Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) classifiers. The dialogues were modified via three specific types of perturbations: (1) synonym replacement, (2) insertion of new sentences, and (3) deletion of existing sentences. The robustness of each extracted conclusion was then re-evaluated using MaxEnt. The effectiveness of this approach was verified across three datasets: two collections of design conversations from the automotive sector and one from the aerospace sector.

This study proposes a novel framework for understanding gravity as a manifestation of a macro-coherent, quantum-correlated holographic vacuum Higgs-Goldstone field that emerges from the collective behavior of post-inflation spacetime. We hypothesize that this field possesses retro-causal properties, linking present matter distributions to future geometric outcomes, with the associated energy flux in the temporal direction serving as the basis for the observed force of gravity. Furthermore, the research examines how the quantum coherence of this field may account for inertial mass through vacuum coherency, while the associated Goldstone mode's interaction with electromagnetic fields offers a mechanism for unifying forces and generating the properties of the proton.

We examine a class of submanifolds within Euclidean space characterized by the property that their associated distance function satisfies both the Descent Lemma and Frank-Wolf's linear constraint qualification. This property encompasses well-known instances such as Euclidean distance on positive definite matrices and more general cases involving arbitrary distances on matrices with fixed rank. We demonstrate that for these groups, Newton's method achieves global convergence with a rate of $O(k^{-2})$, where $k$ represents the iteration count. Furthermore, we present a unified convergence analysis for several first-order algorithms—including proximal point methods, proximal gradient descent, and the proximal Jacobian algorithm—applied to specific problems involving the computation of nearest low-rank matrix approximations.

This study introduces the concept of feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals within associative rings. We establish several characterizing properties and provide full descriptions of such ideals in commutative settings with identity, along with the properties of associated ideal graphs. Additionally, we present specific descriptions describing when the feebly 1-absorbing property holds for primary ideals. The work further examines the relationships between this property and graphs constructed from the inclusion relations among ideals, along with connections to the Zariski topology defined on the ideal graph. The paper concludes by exploring the connections between feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals and the corresponding topological structures in the resulting ideal graphs.

Although astrometric and photometric surveys have successfully mapped millions of stars, their limited spectral data hinders the identification of stellar evolutionary stages and chemical compositions. This study explores how astrometric missions can leverage spectroscopic surveys to build comprehensive stellar catalogs, addressing challenges such as incomplete data, mismatches in coordinate systems, and discrepancies in positional accuracy. We introduce a novel cross-matching strategy that utilizes astrometric photometry to filter candidate matches before conducting spectroscopic comparisons, significantly reducing computational costs. Furthermore, we evaluate the capabilities of the upcoming astrophotonnic missions—specifically PLATO and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope—to perform these tasks, demonstrating that even with a modest number of measured magnitudes, their instruments can effectively derive stellar properties and execute high-performance cross-matching.

Although medication pair therapy is a prevalent form of drug-drug interaction, existing methodologies for assessing these interactions often fail to account for the distinct nature of the pair. This study introduces a relational deep learning approach designed to forecast medication pair scores by utilizing a cohesive framework that integrates both structural and semantic representations. Specifically, medication embeddings are derived from a cohesive graph representation, while pair representations are constructed using context-aware word embeddings. This relational approach was validated through a competition focused on medication pair classification, where it achieved the first-place position.

Identifying road hazards, such as potholes, is crucial for ensuring public safety and maintaining road infrastructure. Although numerous studies have addressed this issue, the majority rely on data from a limited geographic scope, often a single city or nation, which restricts their applicability elsewhere. This limitation stems from the fact that capturing the necessary information typically requires teams of experts to conduct physical surveys across various locations. To overcome this barrier, this study introduces a transfer learning-based framework designed to identify road defects using multispectral remote sensing imagery. By leveraging the pre-trained ResNet50 model, the system achieves strong generalization across different countries, effectively identifying hazards within unseen regions despite being trained on limited-area datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the model's superior performance, reaching an F1 score of 0.9025.

Imitation learning involves a robot acquiring a task from an expert, yet it remains challenging to acquire complex tasks in high-dimensional state spaces, particularly when the expert's policy is implicit within recorded demonstration data. Although recent methods utilizing behavioral cloning and variational inverse reinforcement learning have addressed this, they typically require explicit state features or rely on hand-crafted reward functions. This paper introduces a framework for behavioral cloning that automatically derives a policy directly from raw, multi-sensor observation sequences without manual state definition or reward engineering. By leveraging a latent variable model to capture the underlying state space from historical trajectories, we train the policy using compressed latent representations. We validate the approach across three distinct domains: a simulated robot arm task, a real-world object sorting activity, and a real-world manipulation task involving a beer can.

This study examines the formation of a Population III (Pop III) protostar within a Pop III star cluster, utilizing 3D magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. We find that a prolate magnetic field, initially present in the collapsing Pop III molecular cloud, intensifies exponentially as the cloud contracts. This magnetic field becomes so strong that it halts further fragmentation of the collapsing disk. Consequently, the system forms a protostar accompanied by a relatively flat disk, with the inner region dominated by the amplified magnetic field and the outer region remaining neutral. We estimate that the magnetic field strength at the disk's edge is approximately $10^{-3}$ G, roughly 1000 times stronger than current values observed in Pop III protostars. This intense field could potentially explain the mechanism by which Pop III protostars avoid magnetic disruption.

This study introduces a new repetition-free deduction system tailored for relational association rules, aligning closely with the established Fitting deduction framework. We demonstrate that this repetition-free approach minimizes the number of rules required to derive all semantic consequences of a given database. Additionally, we present a conversion algorithm that generates an equivalent deduction system with the same deductive power but without negations. Finally, we examine the impact of this negation removal on the system's cardinality within relational association rule deduction.

This study examines how mandated mental health treatment influences recidivism among convicted individuals. It posits that, for the general population, acknowledging the link between mental health issues and reoffending supports the implementation of therapy as a sentencing component. Utilizing data from the National Survey of Criminal Justice, the research employs a two-stage approach: first, it assesses the prevalence of psychological disorders within this specific group, and second, it investigates the correlation between court-ordered therapy and reduced recidivism rates. Findings reveal a significant association between conviction and mental illness, with 30% of individuals reporting a diagnosed disorder. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that those subjected to compulsory treatment demonstrate lower recidivism compared to their counterparts not receiving such intervention.

This paper introduces parametric variants of the generalized Apostol–Bernoulli polynomials along with their properties, utilizing an adaptive approach grounded in the Apostol type special polynomials.

This paper introduces a novel approach to wireless spectrum analysis by utilizing autonomous drones to collect radio measurements. The authors present a complete system architecture designed for in-flight spectrum assessment and demonstrate its validation through experiments conducted with a drone-mounted software-defined radio. The study confirms the method's effectiveness through RISE, a machine learning algorithm that estimates comprehensive radio maps by synthesizing sparse flight data. The authors also evaluate the system's performance in terms of coverage and resolution, while exploring applications such as identifying unused frequency bands and performing real-time signal visualization.

This paper introduces a novel method for identifying system anomalies using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). The proposed approach involves monitoring system states via an HMM and calculating the HMM's probability distribution over observed state sequences to detect deviations. The effectiveness of this method is validated through experiments on an artificial system, demonstrating that the Anomaly Identification with HMM (AIDH) framework successfully identifies faults. The results further indicate that the method performs effectively even with limited experimental data.

Biometric authentication has become a critical component of securing personal privacy and sensitive information. This study examines a multimodal authentication system utilizing synchronized video and audio-thermal imagery recorded from human subjects. The system leverages facial recognition derived from visible light video alongside the detection of unique physiological patterns in heat distribution across the face via thermal imaging. Experiments were conducted using a dataset of 1,020 samples from 102 individuals, with each person providing 10 distinct samples. Results indicate that the combined system achieves a detection rate of 99.90% at a false acceptance rate of 0.01%.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) systems frequently face challenges with noisy, accented, or ambiguous audio inputs, which can degrade performance. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective framework designed to improve model robustness against such noise. By leveraging the inherent redundancy in parallel speech data, the method generates synthetic training samples through the combination of multiple annotations. Specifically, we merge the speech tracks from various models to create augmented datasets that feature diverse transcriptions and translations. These enhanced training instances are then utilized to fine-tune ASR and MT systems. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly boosts system performance across diverse acoustic conditions, including but not limited to noisy environments, non-native accents, and low-resource languages.

This study introduces an estimation method for the average of parameters governing a probability distribution within a mixture model. The proposed estimator shares the same target as the standard maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for the corresponding single-component distribution but offers superior performance when that distribution represents a blend of multiple distributions. Specifically, under regularity conditions, the Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimator (GMLE) achieves higher asymptotic efficiency compared to the traditional MLE. The section initially defines this GMLE estimator and examines its theoretical properties, followed by an application to assessing the average annualized sampling error for the U.S. Current Population Survey's monthly Current Population Survey (CPS) data.

While differential privacy is widely regarded as the gold standard for ensuring data confidentiality, it fails to account for the risk that adversaries might infer sensitive information about unrelated individuals due to inherent data correlations. To address this gap, we introduce the framework of one-sided differential privacy, which extends standard differential privacy by incorporating knowledge of dependent traits in the dataset. Formally, this model ensures that the release of query results remains private even when an adversary possesses information on these dependent characteristics. We establish that one-sided differential privacy can be achieved through mechanisms such as the Laplace and exponential distributions applied to independent variables, even in scenarios involving data dependencies. Furthermore, we demonstrate the model's practical relevance by deriving optimal privacy-utility trade-offs for range queries and record linkage tasks in contexts where data correlations are present.

The discovery of a prominent CO gap in the outer regions of the transitional disk AS 209, initially attributed to a planet clearing material, has prompted a re-evaluation of the feature's origin. This study investigates the possibility that the gap results from chemical processing rather than planet formation. We employed radiative transfer and chemical modeling to determine if the CO depletion can be replicated by a viscous, irradiated, and photochemically active gas disk. Our results indicate that a CO gap can indeed be generated through chemical processing, with the specific outcome depending on the disk's physical parameters. We demonstrate that a gas-to-solids ratio of approximately 100 is consistent with the observed CO annulus in AS 209, supporting the hypothesis that the feature arises from gas chemistry. Furthermore, we argue that the coexistence of a CO gap and a bright silicate emission feature at 10 μm in AS 209 provides compelling evidence for concurrent gas and dust processing, suggesting that both phenomena may stem from the same underlying mechanism.

This manuscript introduces a toolkit designed to analyze time-tagged data, a method increasingly prevalent in quantum measurement. The software is written in Python, a language renowned for its versatility in scientific computing, and is released under the permissive MIT License. This licensing allows for both personal and commercial utilization, including modification and redistribution. The tool offers a suite of capabilities for processing raw time-tagged datasets, converting them into histograms, and performing cross-correlation analyses. Furthermore, it enables the tagging of specific events based on auxiliary measurement channels. The toolkit's functionality and utility are demonstrated through two distinct experiments: an electronic one examining the switching dynamics of a single semiconductor spin transistor, and an photonic one analyzing the correlation between photons generated in a quantum dot.

This study focuses on a mean field game involving control-state constrained dynamics, specifically addressing the lack of Lipschitz continuity in the coupling Lagrangian and Hamiltonian with respect to the control variable. The authors establish the presence of "mild solutions" under conditions where the coupling Hamiltonian exhibits only monotonicity regarding control states, a scenario where classical solution methods fail. The approach integrates techniques from control theory with probabilistic analysis, drawing inspiration by the connection between control problems and $\Gamma$-convergence.

Recent high-precision astrometric data from the Gaia mission has revealed that many young stellar clusters within the Milky Way's disk exhibit a filamentary structure. While the prevailing view attributes these "threads" to the cluster's interaction with the galactic tidal field, this study offers an alternative explanation. We demonstrate that a one-armed spiral density wave can generate filamentation in a collisionless stellar system without any direct tidal influence. Furthermore, we show that a one-armed spiral can also produce a two-armed filamentary pattern in the absence of galactic tides, suggesting that observed threads may form independently of the tidal field. Consequently, interpreting these features as evidence of tidal disruption may be misleading, and we urge a re-examination of the physical origins of stellar filamentation.

Discrepancy detection, which involves identifying pairs of objects that do not match, is a fundamental visual task with significant applications in fashion retail, such as removing mismatches in product photography. Although this is inherently a multi-label classification challenge, it has received limited attention from the research community. This paper introduces a novel approach that combines fashion-specific contrastive pre-training with the Transformer architecture. We evaluate various configurations, including both vision-and-language as well as vision-only models, to address the task. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses existing baselines, achieving an AUC of 0.9355 on the specialized Mismatch in Fashion (MIF) dataset. The corresponding source code is publicly available at https://github.com/rohitgarg123/VICTOR.

We present an overview of recent developments in resource theories governing the nonclassicality of light. First, we examine the foundational concepts of these theories, establishing the distinct types of nonclassical resources and the varying degrees of free operations permitted. Subsequently, we survey the current landscape of non-free states and operations, highlighting various frameworks and their respective advantages and disadvantages. Finally, we conclude by suggesting promising avenues for future investigation.

This paper introduces a new asynchronous aggregation approach for federated averaging that utilizes buffer-enabled unconstrained gradient optimization. We prove that the proposed method converges to a stationary point of the global objective function and establish its theoretical convergence rate. Experimental results demonstrate that this algorithm achieves superior performance compared to standard federated learning, particularly in environments with heterogeneous data distributions.

This paper defines a specific calculus framework within algebraically extended polynomial tempered distributions as polynomials in $x$ with coefficients that are operators acting on $x$. We demonstrate that this system satisfies key requirements for being considered "calculus-like," including the ability to differentiate the Dirac $\delta$ function and perform first-order Taylor expansions. Consequently, we establish a corresponding operational method for solving differential equations using these polynomials in $x$.

We investigate the shadow dimension, a concept within the string theory swampland framework, and demonstrate that it imposes an upper limit on the fraction of dark matter attributed to primordial black holes (PBHs). This constraint arises because the shadow dimension alters the expansion history of the universe, thereby modifying the conditions necessary for the stability of the universe against evaporation of a black hole. We further show that this limit is contingent upon the specific scale of the shadow dimension.

This study examines fractures within solid bodies supported by floating shells, a scenario prevalent in geology and materials science. We apply an energetic framework to analyze the system's energy, utilizing the shell's energy functional to derive the equilibrium state and associated energy release rate. Subsequently, we investigate fracture propagation by demonstrating that a system initially bearing a single crack can develop into a periodic array of segments. Finally, we explore the system's response to branching cracks, establishing criteria for when propagation will bifurcate.

The anisotropic strain exerted by lattice-matching substrates significantly influences the electronic properties of GaN. This study employs first-principles calculations to examine how anisotropic strain from ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ affects hole mobility in p-type GaN. Results indicate that aligning the GaN $a$-axis parallel to the $a$-axis of these substrates (GaN//ZnGeN$_2$ or//MgSiN$_2$) induces a negative uniaxial strain, which enhances the valence band edge curvature and boosts hole mobility by up to 1.5 times compared to bulk material. Conversely, a configuration where the GaN $c$-axis aligns with the $c$-axis of the substrates (GaN//ZnGeN$_2$ or//MgSiN$_2$) produces positive uniaxial strain, diminishing hole mobility. Notably, the mobility increase under negative strain is substantially greater for GaN//ZnGeN$_2$ than for GaN//MgSiN$_2$.

This study introduces a new method for efficiently navigating marine robots, addressing the challenge of accounting for how sensor data changes over time. We propose using Sparse Gaussian Process Temporal Variation Learning (SGPTVL) to achieve this, a technique that is both more accurate than standard Gaussian Process Temporal Variation Learning and faster than its Variational autoencoder-based counterpart. The method relies on inducing points to model temporal shifts, a concept that shares similarities with Variational Bayes methods but offers greater computational efficiency. We validate the method's effectiveness through simulations and a practical experiment involving a marine robot tasked with locating a target in a murky environment.

We demonstrate that the Darboux transformation applies to isothermal surfaces represented as meromorphic quadrics. Additionally, we establish an interrelationship between Calapso transformations of the respective surface functions and the (both B\"acklund and Darboux) transformations of the underlying surface.

Or, more directly:

Using the Darboux transformation on quadric surfaces expressed as meromorphic families, we derive an application to isothermal surfaces. We also define how Calapso transformations of associated functions correspond to both B\"acklund and Darboux transformations of those surfaces.

This study introduces a novel nonparametric estimator for conditional expectation functions, $E[Y|X]$. We demonstrate that this estimator achieves the optimal minimax rate of convergence, as established by Kallus (2020), and possesses asymptotic equivalence to the recently proposed estimator by Kallus (2020). Building on this estimator, we propose a method for estimating the Average Treatment Effect on the treated (ATT). We provide theoretical proof that this new ATT estimator is consistent, and simulations indicate that it performs well in practical applications.

This paper presents several new identities concerning the $\lambda$-version of the $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. The work includes multiple summation formulas, a binomial convolution formula, and a corresponding polynomial identity. Additionally, we derive a $\lambda$-version of a well-known identity by Nørlund regarding factorial coefficients and provide the $\lambda$-version of the identity first established by Comtet.

Link forecasting involves predicting emerging relationships within Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKG) and represents a key component of Knowledge Graph completion. Although significant research has focused on this area, most current state-of-the-art methods rely on computationally intensive, dynamic neural network architectures. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel, lightweight, and scalable approach that leverages static embedding techniques. We demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to leading dynamic models while offering substantial improvements in both computational efficiency and memory usage. Additionally, we examine the integration of our static framework with various post-processing strategies to further refine prediction accuracy.

We demonstrate that for morphisms involving row-finite free categories and associated graph algebras, being a robust shift equivalence constitutes a necessary and sufficient condition to be generated by an element within the Groelner group. This result extends an existing theorem by Raeburn and Zhang, which was previously established solely for two-element group actions.

Heavy quark production in high-energy heavy-ion collisions serves as a probe for the strong interaction fields present in the quark-gluon plasma, particularly the intense magnetic fields generated by the colliding nuclei. This study examines how such magnetic fields influence heavy quark imaging through anisotropic fragmentation, employing a general propagator framework to analyze the medium's impact on heavy quark propagation. Our results demonstrate that both the elliptic and triangular flow coefficients, as well as heavy quark transverse momentum spectra, exhibit significant dependence on the specific mechanisms of medium-induced radiative energy loss. Furthermore, we observe that increasing the strength of the external magnetic field enhances flow coefficients while simultaneously suppressing transverse momentum spectra.

Infusing knowledge graphs (KGs) into neural architectures has significantly advanced performance in various natural language processing (NLP) applications. While existing methods effectively integrate KGs for tasks like machine reading comprehension and open-domain question answering, they typically focus on retrieving and mapping explicit information. Conversely, implicit knowledge within KGs often remains underutilized. This study introduces a novel approach that enhances pre-trained language models by incorporating implicit KG data through logical inference. We evaluate this method on the closed-set CoQA and open-set TriviaQA benchmarks, demonstrating that our inference-based framework surpasses current state-of-the-art results.

Expander graphs represent a fundamental concept in combinatorics with numerous significant applications. A primary example involves the Khot-Vishneu's polynomial method, which utilizes high-dimensional expanders to prove the Unique Games Conjecture; notably, existing constructions of these objects rely exclusively on the properties of prime fields. This work presents a novel approach to building high-dimensional expander graphs through covering spaces, yielding a family of examples that are robust against attacks using abelian covers.

Although large language models excel in diverse applications, their ability to perform complex reasoning tasks without assistance remains questionable. This study investigates the effectiveness of using prompt engineering to induce such behaviors in a zero-shot setting, specifically evaluating the choice task—a format requiring the selection of the best answer from multiple options, including cases with multiple correct responses. We examined the impact of different prompt types (e- prompts, direct instructions, and meta- prompts) on performance across single- and multi-select choice tasks involving general knowledge, mathematics, and science. Our findings indicate that while single-select accuracy improves with our proposed prompt strategies, they yield limited gains in multi-select scenarios. Furthermore, we analyzed how these approaches affect performance on specific subject domains and assessed the consistency between model predictions and human judgments.

This paper establishes a general method for defining $\mathscr{L}$-invariants within multiple zeta regularizations and applies this framework to various Artin stem representations. We define these $\mathscr{L}$-invariants as periods of cohomology groups associated with continuous T-continuous Galois representations.

Detecting multiband microwave and terahertz radiation emitted by quantum devices is essential for validating their operation as quantum computers and communication systems. However, conventional detection methods often require specialized equipment, such as vector network analyzers, which are costly and bulky. This study introduces a reconfigurable, multifrequency microwave and terahertz detector based on atomic Rydberg states, enhanced by a deep learning algorithm for superior signal sensitivity. By employing a convolutional neural network to process in-phase and quadrature data, the system achieves a noise-equivalent power of $10^{-12}$ W at 10 GHz, a 10-fold enhancement over standard detection techniques.

We have conducted a detailed analysis of the HI distribution in UGC 8839, a low surface brightness spiral galaxy, revealing a strikingly flat, single-component HI disc. This feature is exceptionally rare, as most spiral galaxies typically exhibit multiple components, including a central bulge and an outer arm. Our observations indicate that the outer component dominates the total HI mass, comprising approximately 95% of the mass, while the inner component accounts for only 5%. Furthermore, the galaxy's HI mass-to-light ratio is exceptionally high, reaching 10.5 $M_{\odot}/L_{\odot}$ (in $I_K$ band), which is more than double the typical value for spiral galaxies. We propose that the extended star formation history in UGC 8839 is responsible for this elevated ratio. Additionally, we detected a significant warp in the HI disc, which may result from a past interaction with a companion galaxy.

Assuming a given quasiregular map is nonuniformly expanding on a specific open subset, the corresponding Hausdorff dimension of that set matches the dimension associated with its unstable cone field. Additionally, for any rational iterate of a rational map, the restricted Hausdorff measure on its Julia set behaves as a measure of maximal Lyapunov weight.

This study examines gravity wave dispersion and motion within Mars's lower thermosphere by analyzing density measurements from four spacecraft: Mars Global Surveyor (MGS), Odyssey (ODY), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), and Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN (MAVEN). The analysis focuses on waves with horizontal wavelengths between 30 and 150 km, occurring in the 110–160 km altitude band, and spanning the 1–10 hour period range. The data reveal that wave phase velocities are generally 100–200 m/s, indicating that dispersion is minimal for waves of this wavelength. The study also assesses wave activity across the four orbital periods, noting a distinct absence of 10-hour period waves in MAVEN observations compared to the other three missions.

Ultra-peripheral collisions (UPCs) in lead-lead systems offer a valuable opportunity to investigate forward J/$\psi$ production, as this process can arise from both the hadronization of quark-gluon pairs and the fusion of photons. This study examines forward J/$\psi$ production in Pb--Pb collisions recorded by the ALICE detector at the LHC, specifically analyzing events with and without extra activity. For the sample containing no additional charged particles, the results are compared against theoretical predictions for exclusive photon-photon collisions. Conversely, for data including extra charged particles, the findings are contrasted with models describing photon-photon interactions alongside gluon-gluon fusion. This analysis aims to determine the relative contributions of these two production mechanisms.

This study introduces a new paradigm for creating audio through visual manipulation, termed VDCSS (Visual Domain Controllable Synthesizer for Sounds). The system allows users to generate sounds within a two-dimensional parameter space, where each axis represents a distinct musical attribute. By employing a 2D grid interface, listeners can explore the auditory results of combining these features at various levels. To support this, the system utilizes a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on a comprehensive dataset of 10,000 human-labeled sounds to map and understand the CNN's internal representations in relation to the specified audio domains. The resulting interface enables precise, granular control over visually guided sound synthesis.

This study introduces a recurrent neural network (RNN) designed to capture temporal dynamics in sequential data. The model, termed the "temporal difference RNN" (TD-RNN), integrates the principles of temporal difference learning (TD) and dynamic programming (DP) to derive sequential temporal knowledge. By employing an optimal policy derived from the $\epsilon$-greedy strategy, the approach effectively mitigates the exploration-exploitation dilemma. The method was validated through experiments on the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), where it demonstrated superior performance compared to standard RNNs and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks.

The severe economic and social consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic have prompted numerous studies on the effectiveness of various non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). However, these analyses frequently rely on specific assumptions about a nation's unique demographics, the inherent characteristics of the virus, and the constraints of the healthcare system. This paper introduces a rigorous, analytical framework that determines the ideal combination of NPIs for any country, regardless of these varying parameters. The proposed solution demonstrates remarkable universality, as it remains stable despite variations in underlying assumptions, thereby offering a robust basis for comparing different countries' pandemic responses.

Machine learning (ML) is increasingly ubiquitous across various industries, driving a growing demand for automated methods to streamline the labor-intensive process of preparing data, features, and models. While recent advancements have focused on enhancing ML efficiency, they often overlook scenarios where the underlying data is flawed. This paper introduces a novel framework for diagnosing issues in data-driven ML pipelines by integrating concepts from cooperative game theory. Specifically, we utilize the Shapley value to assess the significance of data elements in end-to-end systems, offering an exact solution to the significance problem that accounts for the data's marginal impact on ML outcomes. Our approach offers two primary contributions: (1) a mathematical formulation of the significance problem for data elements within the context of data-centric ML, and (2) an efficient algorithm based on the Shapley value capable of handling both tabular and deep learning architectures. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methodology.

This paper examines the challenges and opportunities in contemporary enumerative geometry. The central task of enumerative geometry is to determine the number of solutions satisfying specific constraints within a given geometric context. For instance, it seeks to calculate how many conics are determined by five generic points. Although such problems were foundational in the early development of algebraic geometry, they have recently gained renewed attention due to surprising connections with topology, combinatorics, and physics. The following discussion elucidates these relationships through various statistical and combinatorial models, as well as the study of moduli spaces.

This study investigates the impact of uniaxial pressure on the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn trimerized hexagonal antiferromagnets. Under pressure, the crystal lattice undergoes distortion, triggering a transition from a double-k to a single-k magnetic order. This structural and magnetic shift results in a substantial reduction of the anomalous Hall conductivity, a phenomenon attributed to the collapse of the lattice distortion-induced Berry curvature hotspots. These findings offer valuable insights into the microscopic mechanisms governing the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn.

This study examines the application of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in semantic relation extraction, a task aimed at identifying inter-entity relationships within structured or unstructured data. We overview the complete workflow, beginning with data preparation and preprocessing, followed by the exploration of various DNN architectures used for this purpose. Additionally, we assess current research trends, highlight remaining challenges, and propose potential future directions in the field.

This paper examines a Steklov-Robin type eigenvalue problem defined by the equation $\Delta u + n u = \mu |u|^{p-1} u$ on a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, subject to the boundary condition $\frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu} = u^p + |u|^{p-1}u$ for $u \in H^{1/2}(\partial \Omega)$. The analysis establishes the existence of positive first eigenfunctions and provides the second eigenvalue's algebraic multiplicity is at least two.

We introduce a novel approach to 2D/3D Hypergraph Visual Servoing (HVS) reconstruction, a technique capable of creating both structured and unstructured 3D models from multiple 2D point cloud views containing sparse features. Our method explicitly models the inter-view correspondences of these features as a hypergraph, where cameras act as nodes and feature points form the edges connecting them. By integrating sparse feature tracking with HVS, we simultaneously refine the poses of the views and the 3D positions of the features through sparse optimization. This process iterates until convergence, effectively rebuilding the scene's geometry and the camera trajectory. Furthermore, we employ a guidance strategy that leverages known 6-DoF poses to accelerate convergence and enhance the accuracy of the recovered 3D structure. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm successfully reconstructs complex environments, including those with significant motion blur and visual clutter, from sequences containing sparse features.

Creating annotations for chest radiographs (CXR) is challenging because the imaging process involves significant image degradation, making it difficult to map existing medical records directly. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel strategy that leverages 3D CT scans to generate comprehensive CXR annotations. This method enables the semantic segmentation of organs, the creation of organoid boundaries, and the development of unique identification for pathological findings. We implemented an automated pipeline to produce these semantic segmentations and boundaries, which were subsequently refined through the review of two radiologists. Furthermore, we established a user-friendly interface designed to facilitate the efficient generation of these refined annotations. Evaluated on a dataset of 1,000 CXRs, this system achieved an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.85 for lung segmentation and 0.79 for heart segmentation. Additionally, the system demonstrated 0.84 average precision in detecting pulmonary nodules and 0.81 average precision for identifying pneumonia.

We establish a relationship between the Euler characteristic of minimal thurbon norm surfaces and the Thurstion norm of contact open book decompositions. As a result, we derive constraints on the Thurstion norm for certain contact Thurston norm divisors, demonstrating that specific such divisors cannot exist for tight contact structures on some 3-manifolds.

Microcavity lasers are recognized as promising sources for generating entropic, or random, vectorial light. This study introduces an entropy-based gauge to assess the degree of vectorial randomness in such emissions. The proposed method was validated using microcavity cavity systems, where the results were compared against standard metrics like the Shannon entropy of the wavelength distribution and the spectral autocorrelation. The introduced entropic metric offers a more rigorous evaluation of randomness in both temporal and spatial domains compared to these conventional measures.

This study examines the cost stability of major cryptocurrencies to evaluate their viability as a medium of exchange. By applying the Rietveld and Rietveld (1993) methodology, the research assesses cost stability across Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin, Ripple, and a composite index representing the top 20 cryptocurrencies between 2013 and 2021. The findings indicate that while the cost stability of these digital assets has remained significantly lower than that of the US dollar over the study period, it has shown marked improvement since 2018. This upward trend suggests a growing potential for cryptocurrencies to fulfill an exchange function within the digital economy.

This study examines the stochastic Burgers equation and the associated Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) framework through the lens of inverse scattering, specifically utilizing a time-reversal approach. We demonstrate that a stochastic solution for KPZ can be derived by applying a time-reversed Zakharov-Shabat (ZS) system to an associated operator. This method allows for the explicit calculation of the Darboux transformation and the $\tau$-function for the time-reversed scenario. Furthermore, we establish a direct correspondence between the scattering data of the time-reversed ZS system and the Riemann-Hilbert problem defining a solution to the Cauchy problem for stochastic Burgers' equation. This analysis yields a novel, exact solution to the equation, valid for all $t<0$.

Compressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence is a prevalent feature of the solar wind, characterized by shocklets and current sheets that facilitate efficient particle heating and acceleration. Although the electron-scale dynamics of compressive structures have been examined in detail by the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission, the specific role of electron-scale physics in shaping the overall electron turbulence spectrum remains unclear. This study analyzes MMS data from the solar wind to evaluate the spectral break scale associated with electron kinetics within compressive turbulence. We identify compressive structures using the "compressive factor" derived from the FIELDS instrument's search-coil magnetometer data. Subsequently, we examine the electron spectral breaks within these events using the MMS Electric Field and Double Probe (EDP) data. Our findings indicate that the spectral break frequency scales with the electron gyrofrequency multiplied by the inverse of the structure's duration as measured by MMS. This scaling holds consistently across the majority of analyzed events, with the sole exception of one case.

The generation of isolated attosecond pulses is highly desirable for advancing the temporal resolution of X-ray free-electron lasers (FELs) beyond current limits. A primary obstacle in this endeavor is the inherent polarization instability of standard linearly polarized seed lasers, which drives the radiation of circularly polarized synchrotron light and prevents the isolation of single-axion radiation. We introduce a modified chirp-taper scheme to achieve horizontal polarization control of the x-ray emission. This technique involves applying a time-varying (tapered) horizontal force to the electron beam, which induces a corresponding variation in the radiated frequency (chirping). By analyzing the resulting spectrum using a time-frequency representation, we demonstrate that this approach not only suppresses circular polarization components but also generates a distinct, single-pulse structure.

Gerrymandering remains a critical issue in the United States, where partisan manipulation of district boundaries distorts election outcomes. Although the concept of "packing" and "cracking" is well-understood, existing quantitative metrics often fail to capture the full complexity of real-world redistricting plans. To address this gap, we introduce a new algorithm that generates redistricting maps simulating heat diffusion. By evaluating the temperature variance across districts, this method quantifies the degree of gerrymandering. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to actual congressional districts across various states.

Flaw identification in textiles is critical for the sector, yet existing image-based detection methods often struggle with flaws that share similar textures and hues with the material, leading to subpar performance. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a novel approach specifically for patterned textile inspection. The proposed method employs Fourier decomposition combined with low-rank decomposition to separate flaw signals from the background, utilizing the Gradient Hybrid Orientation Gaussian (GHOG) feature descriptor to capture flaw characteristics. Furthermore, a $\lambda$-based criterion is developed to determine the optimal decomposition parameter. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves superior accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

This work introduces a new approach to first-person visual navigation by combining reinforcement learning with a probabilistic graphical model. Our method employs a hybrid architecture that integrates deep learning components with traditional reasoning, where the latter is driven by the former. Specifically, we utilize a learned policy network to estimate the probability distribution of an agent's trajectory given a sequence of observed images. This estimated distribution feeds into a reinforcement learning process, which optimizes the network to maximize the mutual information between the predicted trajectory and the actual path taken by the agent. By applying this information-theoretic objective, our system effectively balances exploration and exploitation, enabling more efficient navigation in unknown environments. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art visual navigation methods.

We establish a limit on how quickly Bondi mass can decrease within any future-directed causal domain $\Omega$ of a globally hyperbolic spacetime. This theorem applies to Bondi mass defined over future null infinity and is valid for an extensive range of asymptotically flat spacetimes. Our proof utilizes the energy conditions inherent in the stress-energy tensor alongside geometric properties of the null structure. We further demonstrate that this limit is optimal for an asymptotically de Sitter spacetime.

We investigate the generation of gravitational waves from compact object mergers within nuclear star clusters, specifically examining the remnants of Population III stars. Our findings indicate that these clusters can sustain high surface densities of merging compact objects, resulting in gravitational wave luminosity that rivals or surpasses that of active galactic nuclei. Consequently, the first stars in their groupings could become a primary source of gravitational waves.

This paper introduces a novel method for identifying incidents within distribution systems by integrating system models with measurement data. The proposed approach utilizes a data-driven framework to determine the most probable scenario of system states by leveraging historical information regarding incident characteristics and uncertainties. Specifically, it employs dynamic Bayesian networks to account for dependencies between temporal measurements and spatial locations. The effectiveness of this methodology is demonstrated through simulations on the IEEE 123-bus test system.

Furthermore, we determine the branching ratio for $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi \delta$ to be approximately $1.5\times 10^{-4}$, a value consistent with existing measurements.
